Release Notes:
New * MITRE ATT\&CK on every event. DarkStrata now labels each credential exposure with the ATT\&CK techniques it evidences. The add-on extracts them into mitre\_technique\_id, mitre\_technique and annotations.mitre\_attack on both sourcetypes, deduplicated per bundle. * ATT\&CK annotations on all four Enterprise Security correlation searches (mitre\_attack: T1555.003 and T1589.001 on the infostealer searches, T1589.001 on the third-party and critical exposure searches), so notable events and risk objects carry techniques. Short Description:
Ingest DarkStrata credential-exposure threat intelligence into Splunk and Enterprise Security. Detect compromised credentials, infostealer infections and third-party exposure in real time, with CIM-compliant data, ES correlation searches and adaptive-response actions.


Description:
DarkStrata Threat Intelligence Add-on for Splunk brings DarkStrata's credential-exposure intelligence directly into Splunk and Splunk Enterprise Security (ES), so your SOC can detect and respond to compromised credentials before they're used against you. DarkStrata continuously monitors breach data, infostealer/malware logs and third-party exposure for credentials tied to your organisation. This add-on pulls that intelligence into Splunk as structured, CIM-compliant events - ready for correlation, alerting, dashboards and automated response. Use it to: - Detect compromised credentials before they're used maliciously - Identify malware infections through infostealer credential detection - Monitor third-party risk by tracking corporate credentials exposed on external sites - Automate incident response via ES notable events, correlation searches and adaptive-response actions - Enrich threat hunting with credential-exposure context Data is delivered in STIX 2.1 format and mapped to the Authentication and Threat Intelligence CIM data models, so it works out of the box with Enterprise Security's threat-intelligence framework. Collection is incremental and checkpoint-based - only new intelligence is fetched on each run - with configurable batching, rate limiting and connection pooling for predictable performance.

item.title: UK Open Data inputs - v1.0.4 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Release notes: https://github.com/livehybrid/TA-uk-open-data/releases/tag/v1.0.4


Short Description:
Modular inputs for open UK datasets, with a configuration UI. Ingests UK Carbon Intensity (api.carbonintensity.org.uk — half-hourly national intensity + generation mix) and NHS England monthly A&E attendance statistics. No API key. Idempotent, checkpoint-based, safe to run on any interval.


Description:
**UK Open Data** is a UCC-framework built add-on that brings two well-known open UK datasets into Splunk with no API key and no external dependencies beyond outbound HTTPS. **Carbon Intensity** — polls the National Grid ESO Carbon Intensity API (`api.carbonintensity.org.uk`) and indexes, per half-hourly settlement period, the national forecast/actual gCO₂/kWh and intensity band (`carbonintensity:national`) plus the generation mix by fuel type (`carbonintensity:generation`). Ideal for carbon-aware scheduling, ESG dashboards and "greenest time to run" decisions. **NHS A&E (monthly)** — scans the NHS England "A&E Attendances and Emergency Admissions" pages, downloads each monthly CSV you haven't already loaded, and indexes one event per provider plus a national TOTAL row (`nhs:ae:monthly`) — type 1/2/other attendances, 4-hour performance and over-4hr counts. Great for healthcare performance and public-sector analytics. Both inputs are **idempotent**: they checkpoint what they've already indexed, so they're safe to run on any interval without creating duplicates. Carbon re-emits only un-settled recent periods until their actual value lands; NHS only loads months it hasn't seen. Built with the Splunk UCC framework — full configuration UI, per-input index/interval settings, and standard logging.
item.dc:creator: Will Searle

item.title: TrackMe - v2.4.20 [Version Update]
item.description:

Release Notes:
**TrackMe 2.4.20 — a maintenance release for User Activity Monitoring, Cribl Stream and Cribl Edge.** * **User Activity Monitoring: collection no longer stops on same-name knowledge objects.** Splunk can keep a private knowledge object next to a shared one with the same owner, app and name on the same search head tier. The catalog collection refused that pair on every run, so the affected dataset never published again. Both objects are now collected, each with its own identity, and a duplicate never stops a run: it is reported in Collection health instead. See [User Activity Monitoring](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/components_uam.html#pg-components-uam). * **User Activity Monitoring: operations hardening.** Findings-action webhook rules on resolved, dismissed and assigned now fire on operator decisions. A UAM tenant deletion is never refused by its cleanup. A tenant RBAC update reports an incomplete UAM reconciliation instead of a silent success. Clearer wording when reopening a finding of a dismissed Finding group. * **Cribl Stream and Cribl Edge: no more spurious failures when writers overlap.** Report reconciliation and live-run publication wait briefly for the tenant lifecycle guard instead of failing at once, so reports stay reconciled and the evidence no longer lags one interval behind. See [Cribl Stream](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/components_cribl.html#pg-components-cribl) and [Cribl Edge](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/cribl_edge.html#cribl-edge). * **Cribl Stream and Cribl Edge: custom policies.** Write your own SPL policy on the tenant’s Splunk data. Each result row names a Cribl object and opens a finding that behaves like a built-in one: Finding groups, triage, notifications, findings actions and the AI Agent. See [Cribl Stream custom policies](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/cribl_stream.html#cribl-stream-custom-policies-guide) and [Cribl Edge custom policies](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/cribl_edge.html#cribl-edge-custom-policies-guide). * **Findings: bulk actions are fast again.** One request and one transaction per bulk edit, batched Assign to… and Apply rules, cheaper Cribl writes, and webhook deliveries queued in one batch. Automatic webhooks are delivered when the tenant owner is a least-privilege account, and a delivery that keeps failing records why before it is dropped. * **Others.** Bank Holidays hardening: the legacy Maintenance KDB copies purge works from a backed-up register, stale scope rows are removed, a failed scope sync is recorded as such, and VOL keeps its legacy holidays behaviour (see [Bank Holidays](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/ops_bank_holidays.html#pg-ops-bank-holidays)). Tenant Home score action and lag policy modals read the REST response. A dependency refresh with security fixes. See: [https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/releasenotes.html#version-2-4-20-build-1792051492-15-10-2026](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/releasenotes.html#version-2-4-20-build-1792051492-15-10-2026)

item.title: Custom Viz - HTML Renderer - v1.0.7 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Release notes: https://github.com/livehybrid/viz-html-renderer/releases/tag/v1.0.7


Short Description:
Render arbitrary HTML inside a Dashboard Studio panel. Supports `{{field}}` interpolation from search results, theme-aware CSS variables, inline SVG, and optional (off-by-default) script execution. Ideal for branded headers, status badges, rich tables, callouts and bespoke layouts Studio can't otherwise produce.


Description:
Dashboard Studio's markdown panel is deliberately limited — no styled spans, no inline SVG, no data-driven HTML. **HTML Renderer** fills that gap with a custom visualization that renders a HTML template you control, optionally populated from your search results. Use it for branded dashboard headers, "● LIVE" status badges, colour-coded callouts, custom legends, KPI ribbons, inline SVG diagrams/floor-plans, and any rich layout the native panels can't express. Values from the primary data source can be injected with simple `{{field}}` placeholders, so the HTML can reflect live search results (e.g. `Last update: {{latest_time}}`). The renderer is **theme-aware** — it exposes Splunk's CSS variables so your markup automatically matches light/dark dashboards. Script execution is **disabled by default** and only enabled via an explicit, clearly-labelled "Allow Scripts (DANGEROUS)" option, so the default behaviour is safe static HTML. Standard `studio_visualization` custom viz, dependency-free.

item.title: Custom Viz - Realtime Clock - v1.0.8 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Release notes: https://github.com/livehybrid/viz-realtime-clock/releases/tag/v1.0.8


Short Description:
Two animated clock visualizations for Splunk Dashboard Studio: a smooth **analog** clock face (with optional digital readout) and a seven-segment **digital** LCD clock. Timezone-aware, themable colours, optional phosphor glow. No data required — drop one on any dashboard for a live, always-current clock.


Description:
Dashboard Studio has no built-in clock, yet operations walls, NOC status boards, world-clock panels and "as of now" headers all want a live, ticking time display. **Realtime Clock** adds two purpose-built custom visualizations that render the current time entirely client-side at 60fps — no streaming data, no scheduled searches, no backend. **Analog Clock** — a smooth analog face with sweeping hands, tick marks, an optional digital readout and day/date line, and a configurable phosphor glow. Hand, second-hand and tick colours are all configurable. **Digital Clock** — a seven-segment LCD-style display with a blinking colon, 12/24-hour modes, optional seconds, a date line, ghost (unlit) segments for an authentic LCD look, and a phosphor glow. Both support **local time, UTC, or any IANA timezone** (e.g. `Europe/London`, `America/New_York`, `Asia/Tokyo`), so a single dashboard can show a row of world clocks. Because the time is computed in the browser, the clocks stay accurate to the second regardless of search refresh intervals. Built as standard `studio_visualization` custom viz, themable to light/dark, and dependency-free.

item.title: Cisco CDR Reporting and Analytics - v9.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
- **Important** - CUBE legs now join the CUCM legs of the same call only when "merge by ciscoguid" is selected on Investigate > Calls. The old automatic join on the first 8 characters of the guid is gone. - **Important** - This app no longer contains any CUBE configuration. For CUBE data install SA_cube 0.8.0 on the search head and TA_cube 0.8.0 on the indexers. - Removed the old hidden guids and guid_detail views. The guid diagnostics page no longer reports on call_reference_id. - call_reference_id, incoming_call_reference_id and outgoing_call_reference_id are deprecated and no longer used by the app. They are still extracted so saved searches keep working, and will be removed in a future release. - **Functionality** - Major improvements to the conversationId chaining feature. The prior implementation only performed a partial join in some cases. - Merging on Investigate > Calls is now done by a new mergecalls search command, which merges whole calls, follows chains of linked calls of any length, and holds only a few hours of calls in memory at a time. - **Functionality** - New "merge across SME by session id" option on Investigate > Calls (experimental), which joins the legs of a call on either side of an SME by their RFC 7989 session ID. - **Functionality** - New "merge by ciscoguid" option on Investigate > Calls. Unlike the conversationId and session id options it is not CUCM-only: ciscoguid means the same thing on CUCM, CUBE, CVP and SBC records, so it merges a call across clusters and across technologies. - **Functionality** - In all versions of Investigate Calls prior to this release the concurrency and duration_elapsed fields were always empty for every data type except CUCM and CUBE. Both now work for all of them. - **Performance** - The Investigate > Devices page is dramatically faster, commonly 5x to 10x, and more on larger deployments, as a result of eliminating an mvexpand in the SPL. - **Performance** - Investigate > Calls, and every other search that uses the devices lookup, is commonly 2x faster or more, because that lookup no longer allows wildcards. - **Important** - A "*" in the clusterId column of the devices lookup no longer matches any cluster. A new health check lists such rows, and the new App Settings > General page can turn wildcards back on. - **Important** - A CUCM node that is upgraded or reinstalled can reuse old call ids, merging unrelated calls. A new health check finds this, and the new call_id_resets lookup keeps them apart. Each warning includes a search you can run once to record the reset. - On Investigate > Calls, legs of one call that connect in the same second are now always listed in origination order, rather than sometimes in arbitrary order. - On Investigate > Calls, a leg with no value in a text column, or in duration, no longer shifts the values below it up a row, against the wrong leg. For CUBE, use Investigate > Calls. - The Call Detail page now labels legs from the cube_cdr_compact sourcetype with their CUBE direction and activity, as it already did for cube_cdr. - On Investigate > Calls, selecting some but not all clusters no longer hides every CUBE, Oracle SBC and CVP leg. The cluster filters now apply only to CUCM records. - **Functionality** - CVP calls now show on Investigate > Calls with CVP selected, one leg per SIP INVITE, and join their CUCM call under "merge by ciscoguid". Needs SA_cisco_ucce 0.2.0. - **Critical** - On a Splunk Free license the app's first-time-run script never ran at all, because Splunk cannot honor passAuth = splunk-system-user there. None of the app's editable lookups were ever created. - Expanded the field gallery descriptions for the directory URI party fields. - The gallery now also notes that a directory URI whose host is an IP address is the SIP URI as signaled, which incidentally is the same form Expressway, Cisco Meeting Server and SBC records use. - Expanded the gallery descriptions for the RFC 7989 session ID fields and the IMS charging fields (ICID and the IOI pair), which are purpose-built cross- system correlators rather than addresses. - Fixed a bug in the search filters field, where a tab character preceding a field=value searchterm would be handled incorrectly triggering a parse error from splunkd. - The callquality command no longer fails the entire search when call_quality_thresholds.csv is absent. It matched the zero-padded call_reference_id against the guid text, which is not padded. - The call detail page now finds a call's CUBE legs by ciscoguid. Before, a CUBE leg reached through a CUCM trunk-to-trunk leg was missing there, even when Investigate Calls showed it. - The call detail page has its own data type selector, set from Investigate Calls, and brings in a call's records from every selected system that carries its ciscoguid: CUBE, Oracle SBC, CVP, UCCE and CCCSP. - On Investigate Calls, a call that went through CUCM and an Oracle SBC now has one "view call details" link, to the main call detail page, as CUBE calls already did. The Oracle SBC detail view remains for calls that never touched CUCM. - The call flow diagram on the call detail page now draws a call's Oracle SBC and CUBE hops alongside its CUCM legs, with each box named the way it is named in CUCM. - In the call detail page's legs table, every non-CUCM row now gets the alternate background, the note above the table names which systems those rows came from, and data_type is now a default column. - The "other data sources" panel on the call detail page now also searches the app's own indexes, and recognizes a call's ciscoguid in each of the forms those systems write it. - Fixed a bug where if you had the conversationId merging option on, CUBE and Cisco Meeting Server legs fell out of any call that merged, and showed up as a separate call carrying a CUCM call id. - The health checks for required Splunk and app versions are now one check each, covering every installed Sideview app, in place of the eight near- identical copies the apps used to ship. item.description:

Release Notes:
Three defects. Certificate verification was not being applied to the app's HTTPS requests, because Splunk's own default makes Python's default context unverified and the app relied on that default; it now builds a verified context itself. The PolyScore tile on the Triage page coloured a convicted URL, domain or address green, because it banded from a score the platform returns as a constant for those types; it now follows the engine detections. Upgrading: a search head behind a middlebox that terminates and re-signs TLS was being accepted silently and will now be refused. Short Description:
PolySwarm malware threat intelligence and file reputation for Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud Platform. Hash lookup and IOC enrichment for MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, URLs, domains and IP addresses: crowd-sourced verdicts from many engines, malware family attribution, sandbox detonation, an opt-in threat intel feed and a matching search.


Description:
The PolySwarm App integrates crowd-sourced malware threat intelligence into Splunk by enriching indicators of compromise, or IOCs, with verdicts derived from multiple detection engines. It is a file reputation and hash lookup source for the SOC: the app processes MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, URLs, domains and IP addresses found in Splunk events, annotating them with threat scores, verdict classifications, and detection counts sourced from the PolySwarm platform. It extracts and refangs indicators from raw text fields within the search head environment, at no cost and with no API key, and submits artifacts to a cloud-based sandbox for behavioral analysis. Search results are augmented with metadata including malware family attribution, file type classification, and aggregated security vendor assessments. The app operates entirely on the search head tier and relies on a key-value store to cache verdict data, track sandbox task state, and maintain modular input checkpoints. Enrichment occurs through five specialized search commands that query the PolySwarm API: the indicators being looked up are sent to PolySwarm, and nothing else from the deployment is transmitted. A local verdict cache means a repeated indicator costs nothing, and every metered request carries an explicit ceiling. Deployments whose search heads reach the internet through a proxy can route this traffic through it, with credentials held in encrypted storage and certificate verification always enforced. Events tagged with the polyswarm:artifact source type represent threat intel pulled from the PolySwarm feed and from sandbox task results, and each one carries the artifact's MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 so it can be matched against events however your own sources log a digest. A saved search ships with the app, disabled by default, that correlates those indicators against your events and carries the verdict, score, family attribution and report link through to the alert, so an analyst sees why a match matters rather than only that one occurred. It reads indexed events only and consumes no PolySwarm quota. Three dashboards cover enrichment activity and entitlement, sandbox detonations, and per-indicator triage, and opening any of them is free because no panel calls PolySwarm. Four workflow actions give an analyst one-click enrichment from a search result's field menu, enrichment with attribution, direct navigation to the PolySwarm portal, and the triage page opened on that indicator.

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
\- Search compact events by writing the \`tx\` macro in front of an ordinary search: \`\`index\=app\_logs \`tx\` "payment failed" NOT retry status\=500\`\`. It runs as native SPL in the search bar, Dashboard Studio panels, saved searches and alerts, and passes Splunk's risky-command check. The words after it behave as on the original lines; \`earliest\=\` and \`latest\=\` go before it, and a time modifier or an unquoted comma after it stops the search with a message. The \`tx\` and \`tenxsearch\` commands keep working for saved searches written with them. \- The template collection is replicated to the indexers with the knowledge bundle, so expansion runs on the indexers instead of the search head. \- Template records are read at search time instead of being stored in the index files a second time. \- The \`tx\`, \`tenx-events\` and \`tenx-templates\` macros are shared with every app.


Short Description:
Send Splunk the logs that sampling and filters keep out to fit the license, on that same license. Compact events take a fraction of the volume and expand back byte-identical at search time; classic dashboards keep their SPL, and one command covers the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API.


Description:
With the Log10x App, Splunk can index compact log events and still search, chart and alert on the original lines. The 10x Receiver stores each event as a template hash plus the values that change, so a stream of repeated patterns takes less of the license. On the OpenTelemetry demo, Splunk's license meter counted 63.91% fewer bytes, encoded events and templates included, and every line expanded back byte-identical with the Receiver settings in the installation steps (measurement: https://github.com/log-10x/benchmarks/tree/main/splunk-license). The same license then holds more: sources that were sampled, filtered or kept out of Splunk to stay under the limit can come back, or the license can be smaller. Classic dashboards keep their SPL: the browser sends each panel's search to the app, which rewrites it on the server. From the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API, a search is wrapped in the tx command (tenxsearch also works). An alert created in the app's Compile Alert view is compiled once into a native saved search, so the scheduler runs no Python. NOT, OR, groups, phrases, field conditions, and values such as IP addresses and hostnames behave as they do on the original data. The 10x Receiver produces compact events, and it is free on up to 10 nodes (https://www.log10x.com/pricing). No sign-up is required to evaluate it: with no license token it runs the full product for 30 days on up to 10 nodes, air-gapped, and a free license removes the time limit (https://doc.log10x.com/manage/license/). The app itself is open source under the MIT license.

Description:
Bitdefender GravityZone Data Collector brings GravityZone security incidents and console activity into Splunk. GravityZone incidents do not stand still: alerts are added, more endpoints become involved, severity changes, and analysts assign, prioritise, comment on and close them. The add-on collects that whole history, so you can triage, investigate and report on GravityZone incidents alongside the rest of your security data. It collects two kinds of data through the GravityZone API, one input per GravityZone company, so a single Splunk deployment can follow many companies, as partners and managed service providers need. The first is security incidents, both endpoint (EDR) and extended (XDR): every time an incident changes, the add-on indexes the new version with a field-level diff and a short, readable summary of what changed. The second is console activity: every entry of the company's GravityZone user activity log, such as sign-ins and failed sign-ins, changes to users and companies, tasks, quarantine actions and actions on incidents, each indexed as its own searchable event. Actions on incidents are also linked to the incidents they affected. Four dashboards are included. Incident Overview shows what is open, how serious it is, who owns it, who initiated it and what GravityZone did about it. Incident Changes is a filterable feed of changes, with severity and priority escalations and re-opened incidents. Incident Detail shows the current state and full history of one incident, with its alerts, nodes and notes, the incidents GravityZone grouped with it, and who changed it in the console. SLA and Ingestion Health shows the time taken to assign and to resolve incidents, open work by owner, and whether every input is collecting. The dashboards focus on incidents; the complete console activity log is available to your own searches, selected by gz_event_type=activity_log. All data uses the bitdefender:gravityzone sourcetype, with plain summary fields named gz_* that keep your own searches simple and fast.

Release Notes:
To keep **searches responsive** over large modules (e.g. `logarchive`), the Addon extracts a selected set of high-value fields at **index time** for the `digit:saf:parseddata:json` source type only. These fields are stored in the index and and bring a massive performance gain when searching. The index-time fields are prefixed with `saf_idx_` (underscores only) so their names are unique, valid as indexed field keys, and never collide with the search-time `KV_MODE = json` fields. The original (un-prefixed, dotted) names remain available at search time via `KV_MODE = json`, but don't benefit from the speed. **For a given field you therefore have two names: use the `saf_idx_` name for fast filtering and `| tstats`, and the plain name (e.g. `data.process`) for everything else.** Indexed fields (12): `saf_idx_module`, `saf_idx_case_id`, `saf_idx_timestamp_desc`, `saf_idx_data_event_type`, `saf_idx_data_log_type`, `saf_idx_data_euid`, `saf_idx_data_boot_uuid`, `saf_idx_data_process`, `saf_idx_data_pid`, `saf_idx_data_subsystem`, `saf_idx_data_category`, `saf_idx_data_library`. Notes: * **Filtering** on an indexed field is faster transparently (e.g. `saf_idx_data_process=mussel`). **Aggregating** fast requires `| tstats` (e.g. `| tstats count by saf_idx_data_process`); a `search ... | stats` still scans raw events. Trailing wildcards (`keyword*`) use the index; leading wildcards (`*keyword`) do not. * Index-time fields apply only to data indexed **after** this config is in place. To benefit on existing cases, perform a one-time clean + reingest. New cases get the fields automatically. * **Scope:** because the indexed names carry the `saf_idx_` prefix, they are unique to this TA. `fields.conf` (`INDEXED = true`) applies only to these `saf_idx_*` names, so it does not affect the plain `KV_MODE = json` fields or any unrelated data on the same instance.

The eollookup search command takes a product and a version from each row and adds: - whether the version is still supported, close to its end, or past end of life - the end-of-life date, with days remaining or days past - the EOL Risk Score (0 to 100) and its letter grade - whether the product has an entry in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog - where the date comes from, as a link you can open Full patch versions work: 18.19.0 is answered for the Node.js 18 line, 8.6 for RHEL 8. When a build could belong to more than one support line (SQL Server service packs, Firefox standard and ESR) the app does not pick one. It says so and lists the candidates. Nothing is guessed. Included: - eollookup, a streaming search command that batches lookups, so a search over many hosts makes few API calls - an overview dashboard: past end of life, ending within 180 days, past end of life with a CISA KEV entry, and rows that could not be matched - four example reports, none scheduled - a setup page that stores your API key in Splunk's encrypted credential store Coverage is 500+ products: operating systems, databases, language runtimes, frameworks, network and security appliances. Every date names its source. What leaves your environment: product names and version strings, sent over HTTPS to api.endoflife.ai when the command runs. No host names, users, IP addresses or event data. The app works without an API key at the anonymous limits, which is enough to evaluate it. Keys and their limits are published at https://endoflife.ai/api.

Version 2.0.0 2.0.0 is a major release. It changes the event format, so read "Upgrading from 1.1.x" before you upgrade. NEW * Cyber feeds: the input now also collects Luminar finished intelligence reports and the threat actors, campaigns, malware, vulnerabilities (CVEs), targeted sectors and locations they cover. * New event format: one JSON event per STIX object, with ready-to-use IOC fields (ioc\_type, ioc\_value, ip, domain, url, file\_hash, email), the feed name (luminar\_feed) and Luminar context such as luminar.score. * Lookups: ten saved searches build lookups after each collection. They include active IOCs (KV Store) with expiry and a minimum score (luminar\_min\_score macro, default 60), IOC attribution to threat actors and malware, report context, a domain lookup that also matches subdomains, CVE intelligence with Luminar exploitation flags and CVSS, and leaked accounts. * Detection rules: six correlation searches, shipped disabled. They cover connections to malicious IPs, web requests to malicious URLs, malicious file hashes on endpoints, DNS queries to malicious domains and their subdomains, successful logins by leaked accounts, and scanner CVEs that Luminar reports on. * They read the CIM data models by default; each rule's log-source macro can point it at your own data instead. * In Splunk Enterprise Security they appear as correlation searches, with the notable event settings already filled in. * Alert history: the detection rules write every alert to the luminar\_alerts index. The new Detection Matches dashboard shows them by rule, severity, threat actor, malware and affected asset. * Allowlist: stop alerts on known false positives, such as CDN IP addresses or test accounts, for all rules or one rule, with an expiry date and a reason. * New dashboards: Threat Intel Overview, Threat Profiles, Leaked Credentials, Cyberfeeds, Luminar Report, Ingest Health, Detection Matches, Allowlist and Log Sources. The Main Dashboard adds cyber feeds panels and an ingest-time filter. * Field menu actions: look up an IP address, domain, URL, file hash, account or CVE in Luminar from any search result, and open threat actor, malware and campaign profiles and reports. * New input settings: * "Mask Leaked Passwords", on by default: leaked passwords keep only their first and last character, and the clear text is never written to Splunk. * "Rebuild Lookups After Collection", on by default. * Credentials are checked when an input is saved. If Luminar rejects them, or the host cannot be reached, the input is not saved and the reason is shown on the form. CHANGES AND FIXES * Each feed keeps its own checkpoint, so an interrupted run resumes from its last batch. * Indicators that have already expired when they are collected are no longer ingested. * Deleting an input also deletes its checkpoints, so an input re-created with the same name starts from its initial fetch date. * Searches, lookups and the new dashboards read the Luminar index through the luminar\_index macro (default: index\=main). UPGRADING FROM 1.1.x 1. Review your own searches, reports and alerts on Luminar data. Events are now one per STIX object, with new field names (for example, indicator\_type is now ioc\_type). Events collected by 1.1.x keep their old format. 2. If your input writes to an index other than main, set the luminar\_index macro to that index (Settings > Advanced search > Search macros). 3. Existing inputs continue from their 1.1.x checkpoint; you do not need to re-create them. The new cyber feeds start from the same point. 4. The lookups and dashboards fill after the first collection that follows the upgrade. To build them sooner, run the saved searches "Luminar - 01" to "Luminar - 10" in order. 5. To use the detection rules: a. Create the luminar\_alerts index. b. Point the rules' log-source macros at your data (the Log Sources dashboard tests them). c. Enable the rules. See "Detection rules" in the README. REQUIREMENTS * Splunk Enterprise with Python 3.13 (tested on Splunk Enterprise 10.6), with the KV Store enabled. * Optional, for the detection rules as shipped: the Splunk Common Information Model add-on and CIM-mapped data. item.description:

Release Notes:
**Splunkbase AppInspect fixes** * Cleared the "public IP `3.57.65.44`" rejection. There is no address: SVG path data lets numbers run together, because a second decimal point always begins a new number, so that run is the three coordinates `3.57`, `0.65` and `0.44`. All 20 hits came from icon artwork inside Excalidraw. * The build now separates those runs at a boundary the parser already recognised, leaving rendering untouched — across the 14 affected paths the parsed number sequences are identical before and after. `scripts/space-svg-path-numbers.py` is confined to `d="..."` attributes and **fails the build** if an IP-shaped string survives outside path data. * Removed `[install] state_change_requires_restart`, which forced a splunkd restart on every enable/disable. No `[triggers]` stanza replaces it: that is only for an app's own custom conf files, and configuring it for `collections.conf`/`transforms.conf` is itself an AppInspect failure. **Shape library** * Inserts as **SVG Icon** by default, listed first, with *Elements* relabelled **Text**. Sticky notes and zones have no icon artwork and still insert as editable elements. * The toggle row wraps instead of compressing: `all: unset` strips the buttons' sizing, so without `flex-shrink: 0` the label spilled out of its own highlight.


Short Description:
Collaborative Excalidraw whiteboard inside Splunk for platform architecture and workshop diagrams. Splunk shapes, example boards, and KV Store persistence — no external infrastructure.


Description:
Whiteboard App is a native Splunk canvas for architecture and workshop diagrams — no external database or middleware. Draw inside Splunk Web with Excalidraw, Splunk infrastructure shapes, and ready-made example boards; boards persist in KV Store. New boards are private by default; share with everyone on the instance when you are ready. Export PNG/SVG/JSON or walk through designs step-by-step in Present mode. Built for architects, SEs, and facilitators who sketch where their audience already works. Requires Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud (Victoria) 9.0.0 or later.
